---
title: "Marks and Auras: Position and Reach"
---

A record can contain more variation than one glance can hold. We choose a point to orient ourselves, then describe how far the values reach around it.

The presentation calls these roles **mark** and **aura**.

## 🔰 A mark answers a question about position {#sec-sample-marks-and-auras-a-mark-answers-a-question-about-position}

Use the record

$$
S=(1,2,2,5).
$$

Different questions choose different marks:

- **Minimum:** where does the observed range begin? At one.
- **Maximum:** where does it end? At five.
- **Mean:** where do the values balance? At $(1+2+2+5)/4=2.5$.
- **Median:** where does ordering divide the record into halves? At two.

The mean need not be an observed value. The median and the mean need not coincide.

A mark gains meaning through its selection rule.

## 🏵 The mean is a balance point {#sec-sample-marks-and-auras-the-mean-is-a-balance-point}

For $n>0$ numerical observations,

$$
M_{\mathrm{mean}}(S)=\frac1n\sum_tS[t].
$$

Subtracting this mark leaves deviations whose total is zero:

$$
\sum_t(S[t]-M_{\mathrm{mean}})=0.
$$

For our record, those deviations are $(-1.5,-0.5,-0.5,2.5)$. Their positive and negative contributions balance.

That is why the mean responds to a large value far from the others: a distant observation exerts more influence on this balance.

## ⚙️ The median uses order {#sec-sample-marks-and-auras-the-median-uses-order}

For a probability law, a median $m$ satisfies

$$
\mathbb P(X\leq m)\geq\frac12,
\qquad
\mathbb P(X\geq m)\geq\frac12.
$$

For a finite sample, apply this to its relative counts. At least half the observations lie on either side, counting equality on both sides.

A discrete cumulative distribution can jump over $1/2$. Requiring exact equality would exclude perfectly ordinary medians.

For an even number of observations, taking the midpoint of the two central ordered values gives a conventional choice. Other median values can be possible when those central values differ.

## 💡 An aura needs a declared measure {#sec-sample-marks-and-auras-an-aura-needs-a-declared-measure}

For our record, the full range is

$$
A_{\mathrm{range}}=\max S-\min S=5-1=4.
$$

This is a difference between values. It is not the observation count and not the count of integers from one through five.

A five-mark description uses the minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile, and maximum. With the **median-of-halves convention** for this four-value record,

$$
(1,\ 1.5,\ 2,\ 3.5,\ 5)
$$

gives those marks. The interquartile aura is then

$$
A_{\mathrm{IQR}}=3.5-1.5=2.
$$

Quantile conventions can differ, especially for small records. Naming the convention makes the result reproducible.

A standard-deviation aura answers another question: how large are deviations around the mean in a root-mean-square sense? [Signal Energy](signal-energy.qmd) develops it from that question.

## ☯ A summary is an intentional loss {#sec-sample-marks-and-auras-a-summary-is-an-intentional-loss}

The notation $P(M)\{A\}$ retains a profile alongside a mark and an aura. If we keep only $M$ and $A$, the profile is usually not recoverable.

For example, the records

$$
(-1,-1,1,1)
\quad\text{and}\quad
(-\sqrt2,0,0,\sqrt2)
$$

share mean zero and empirical variance one. Their shapes differ.

Knowing where a signal balances and how far it typically spreads does not determine which values are common.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try the idea {#sec-sample-marks-and-auras-try-the-idea}

Replace five by 50 in $S=(1,2,2,5)$. What happens to the mean, median, and range? Explain which definition makes each response happen.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Work it through {#sec-sample-marks-and-auras-work-it-through}

The mean becomes $55/4=13.75$, because the balance must respond to the larger value. The median stays two because the central ordered values stay two. The range becomes $50-1=49$ because it follows the endpoints.
:::
